summary: A summary report of a one-day Chatham-House-rule discussion between three NSF S3C2 researchers and 12 participants from 6 unnamed US government agencies (July 2025) on supply-chain security: SBOM/VEX/compliance, vulnerable dependencies, malicious commits, build infrastructure, culture, LLMs, and component choice. Each section lists 'continued themes' and 'new ideas' from the notes; there is no data collection instrument beyond moderator questions (Appendix A).

claims.claim: Government practitioners now treat LLM-based systems 'as software' (CVEs/CWEs apply) rather than as a new category.
claims.evidence: §7.2 'AI as Software' paraphrases unattributed participant remarks; no count of how many participants held the view.

claims.claim: SBOM adoption is stalled by missing incentives/enforcement, trust in produced SBOMs, and vendor pushback; VEX adoption is low due to legal-liability concerns.
claims.evidence: §2.1-2.2 narrative summaries of discussion; consistent with prior S3C2 summits but no independent data.

claims.claim: Participants want paved paths (curated components/containers) to make secure choices the default.
claims.evidence: §8.1 single short paragraph citing vendor examples mentioned by participants.

patterns.note: Discussion of policy/compliance as the driver of security controls; not agent-specific.
'Isolating builds' mentioned as continued theme (§5.1); no agent sandbox content.
MCP mentioned only as a shift in model architecture assumptions (§7.2).

methodology.sample: 12 participants from 6 US government agencies, one day; identities/affiliations withheld (Chatham House).
methodology.baselines: n/a (qualitative report); comparisons to prior S3C2 summits are narrative.
methodology.variance: n/a; no indication of how many participants supported each point.

standards.peer_review: None indicated (no arXiv comment/journal_ref); report reviewed by summit participants and other S3C2 authors (§1).
standards.artifacts: Discussion prompts in Appendix A; no transcripts or coding.

biases.detail: Invited participants 'invested in software security'; topics chosen by participant vote; attendance intentionally capped.
Notes taken by three researchers and drafted by a PhD student; no coding scheme, inter-rater agreement, or frequency of views.
Abstract says 'Thursday, July 9th' and 'six topics'; §1 says 'Wednesday, July 9th' and 'seven topics' (§9 lists seven).

coi.affiliations: NC State, Paderborn/George Washington, U. Maryland, CMU (S3C2 academic center).

verdict_reason: Anecdotal, unattributed practitioner discussion summary with no systematic qualitative method and internal inconsistencies; LLM content (§7) is generic (hallucinated packages, poisoning, 'amnesia') and says nothing about agent harness design. Off-topic for harness decisions beyond background supply-chain context.
applicability: Little transfers. For a Java backend team the only usable signals are background: hallucinated-package risk argues for dependency allow-lists / lockfile and SBOM checks on agent-generated Maven changes across the several repositories, and 'paved path' supports a single shared harness config across mixed agent hosts. None of this is evidence; it does not inform spec-driven development.
